clinicalPearls: Inflammation centred on the subareolar ducts, typically affecting younger women in contrast to the older women affected by duct ectasia.
Very strongly associated with cigarette smoking, which is central to both causation and recurrence.
Presents with periareolar pain, inflammation, a tender subareolar mass or a recurrent non-lactational abscess.
Recurrent infection may discharge through the areolar margin and establish a mammary duct fistula between a subareolar duct and the skin.
Nipple retraction at the site of the affected duct can develop and may mimic malignant retraction.
Although classed as an inflammatory rather than infective process, secondary infection is often mixed, including anaerobes.
Acute episodes are managed with antibiotics active against anaerobes and drainage of any abscess, ideally by aspiration.
Definitive treatment of recurrent disease or fistula is total (major) duct excision, and smoking cessation is essential to reduce recurrence.
reference.pathophysiology: Periductal mastitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the large subareolar ducts distinct from involutional duct ectasia. Damage to the duct epithelium, strongly linked to the toxic and ischaemic effects of cigarette smoke, allows leakage of ductal secretions into surrounding tissue and provokes a periductal inflammatory response. Secondary bacterial colonisation, frequently mixed aerobic and anaerobic, leads to recurrent subareolar abscess formation. Repeated inflammation and drainage through the areolar margin can create an epithelialised track, the mammary duct fistula, and periductal fibrosis may cause nipple retraction. Persistent smoking perpetuates the cycle and underlies the high recurrence rate.
additionalDifferentials: Sebaceous or epidermoid cyst with infection
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment including detailed smoking history
Ultrasound of the subareolar region to detect an abscess or fistula
Aspiration of any collection with microbiological culture including anaerobes
Mammography in older patients or when malignancy is a concern
Core biopsy of any persistent mass or if inflammatory carcinoma is suspected
Fistulography or examination under anaesthesia for a suspected duct fistula
Skin swab and pus culture to guide antibiotic choice
redFlags: Failure of an inflammatory episode to resolve, raising concern for inflammatory carcinoma
A persistent hard mass after resolution of inflammation
Diffuse skin oedema and peau d'orange
Recurrent abscess with an established mammary duct fistula
reference.prognosis: Periductal mastitis is benign but notoriously prone to recurrence, particularly if smoking continues; established fistulae frequently recur until the affected duct system is excised. With smoking cessation and appropriate surgery the long-term outlook is good.
pitfalls: Confusing periductal mastitis in a young smoker with involutional duct ectasia
Overlooking anaerobic cover when treating a non-lactational abscess
Repeated incision and drainage that promotes fistula formation instead of definitive duct excision
Mistaking non-resolving inflammation for infection and missing inflammatory carcinoma
Neglecting to address smoking, the key driver of recurrence
references: Standard textbook of breast surgery on non-lactational infection
National guidance on management of breast abscess and mastitis
management: Promote and support smoking cessation as the cornerstone of treatment, since cigarette smoke drives both causation and recurrence
Treat active infection with antibiotics covering mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms, such as co-amoxiclav or a combination including metronidazole
Drain a subareolar abscess by needle aspiration or incision, sending pus for microbiological culture including anaerobes
Excise the diseased duct system (total duct excision or fistulectomy) for an established mammary duct fistula or recurrent disease
Exclude malignancy with imaging and core biopsy in older patients or where a persistent mass or nipple retraction mimics carcinoma
Provide analgesia and counsel on the high recurrence rate if smoking continues, and refer to breast surgery for recurrent or complicated disease
